tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 08:00 to 09:00 on a clear winter morning, any day except Monday when the palace is shut. November light is crisp but the wind is sharp: hat, gloves and layers.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Roughly four kilometres of flat walking plus security queues; high thresholds and staircases inside the palace, and a steep stepped climb (about a hundred steps) up Jingshan.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Individual credits appear under each stop's photograph.
tour.overviewText:
Stand on an empty pedestrian street at eight in the morning, breath smoking, a grey fortress gate filling the sky — and you are standing on the middle line of a capital that has measured itself from this spot for six centuries. This walk follows that line due north, and it is the straightest history lesson in China.

Beijing matters because emperors made it the centre of the world and modern China kept it that way. The Ming — the dynasty that ruled China from 1368 to 1644 — moved the capital here, and its Yongle Emperor raised the Forbidden City palace between 1406 and 1420; the Qing, the Manchu dynasty of 1644 to 1912, inherited it. The palace sits on a south-north axis because the cosmos demanded it: the emperor, calling himself the Son of Heaven, faced south toward warmth and light while his subjects bowed facing north, and the city was laid out by feng shui — literally wind-and-water, the old rules for siting buildings so fortune flows kindly. Around the axis grew the hutong city: hutong (say hoo-tong) means the narrow lanes of courtyard houses, siheyuan, where extended families lived around four wings and a tree. Outsiders picture Beijing as temples or smog. It is both, plus dry-humoured, and the halves share every pavement.

Today's Beijing is a megacity of more than twenty-one million, paid for by government, tech and universities. The danwei — the old socialist work units that once housed and employed their members for life — are mostly gone, but their compounds still shape how neighbours know each other. Politics is never off this route: Mao proclaimed the People's Republic from the gate tower in 1949, the square below was rebuilt oversized in 1958–59, and in 1989 it filled with student-led protests that ended in a military crackdown, an event commemorated abroad and unmentionable in public here. Redevelopment runs through the day, and wherever it does this tour says so in one breath — supporters call it renewal, critics mourn what was demolished — and moves on.

The shape of the walk is a single straight line. You start at the old front gate in the south, cross the great square, pass through the palace's outer court of throne halls, slip out its back gate, and finish on the hilltop where the whole axis lies below you — roughly four kilometres, half a day with queues.

Practicals, because November is honest. Mornings hover near freezing and the wind cuts across the squares, so wear a hat and gloves; afternoons can be brilliantly clear or hazily smoggy. The palace is closed on Mondays — never plan this walk for one — and you must book its ticket online days ahead with your passport (about ¥40 in the low season; ¥ is the yuan, China's money, formally called renminbi). The square is free but needs its own advance reservation plus a security check, and you will show your passport all day, so carry it. Verify every price at the gate, because they move. Hot noodles wait at both ends of the line.

Walk it slowly. Every gate you pass was a rank, every roof a rule, and the hill at the end explains them all.
tour.summary: One straight line up the middle of Beijing: old front gate, giant square, palace throne halls and the hilltop panorama, in about four kilometres.
tour.title: Beijing – Imperial Axis: Qianmen to Jingshan

stops.accessibility: Level pedestrian street, mostly smooth. The gate-tower museum has stairs and no lift.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The street is free at all hours. The gate-tower exhibition is ticketed (about ¥20 at last check); verify prices at the gate.
stops.insiderTip: Slip one block east into Dashilan West Street: the preserved shopfronts there are older than anything on the rebuilt main strip.
stops.name: Qianmen Street & Zhengyangmen Gate
stops.narration:
Start with your back to the old city and your face to a wall of grey brick forty metres wide. That is Zhengyangmen — the Front Gate — and the straight avenue running south from it is Qianmen Street. You are standing on the middle line of Beijing, and everything today runs north from here.

Here is the mechanism the whole walk depends on. Old Beijing was two walled cities: the Inner City, home to the Manchu bannermen (the hereditary soldier families of the Qing, the Manchu dynasty that ruled China from 1644 to 1912), and the Outer City, where Han Chinese merchants lived. Han means the ethnic majority of China. This gate was the door between them, and through it passed taxes, tribute, examinees and coffins. A gate was never just a door. It was a customs post, a billboard and a threat, and its height told every arrival exactly how small they were.

Now look at the street itself with clear eyes. The grey facades, the tram rails, the republic-era shop signs — most of it was rebuilt in the run-up to the 2008 Olympics, after the original lanes were cleared. Supporters call it renewal, a rescue of a slum; critics call it a stage set and mourn the hutong neighbourhoods demolished to build it. Hutong (say hoo-tong) means the narrow lanes of old Beijing, lined with siheyuan — courtyard houses where extended families lived around four wings and a tree. Hold both views as you walk. The new street is pleasant and the grief is real.

The street costs nothing and never closes. The gate-tower museum is ticketed, about ¥20 at last check — ¥ means yuan, the unit of Chinese money (the currency is called renminbi, and people say kuai, like bucks) — but verify prices at the gate, because they move.

Walk north up the pedestrian strip, under the gate's shadow, about ten minutes to the square's security entrance. Keep your passport handy. You will show it all day.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north up the pedestrian street, pass under Zhengyangmen Gate, and continue about 700 metres to the Tiananmen Square security checkpoint at the square's southern end. Have your passport and reservation ready for inspection.
stops.openingHours: Street open at all hours. Gate-tower exhibition roughly 09:00 to 16:00, Tuesday to Sunday; verify locally.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: TarnishedPath, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Vast flat paving, fully level. Expect long slow security queues with no seating.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Entry is free but since 2021 you must reserve online in advance and pass a security check with your passport. Slots go fast on weekends; verify the booking rules before you come.
stops.insiderTip: At dawn the flag-raising draws a silent crowd; the time equals local sunrise and the square opens extra early for it.
stops.name: Tiananmen Square
stops.narration:
Step out of the checkpoint funnel and stop. Let the scale land. The paving runs nearly a kilometre north to the gate tower, and the square covers about 440,000 square metres — room, the guides say, for a million people standing shoulder to shoulder. It is among the largest public squares on earth, and its size is the message.

This was not always here. In the 1950s this ground was still lanes, ministries and a walled corridor leading to the palace. In 1958–59 the new government cleared it all and laid the square out ten times bigger, flanked by the Great Hall of the People and the National Museum — two of the Ten Great Buildings raised in a single year for the tenth anniversary of the People's Republic. That is the mechanism: a state that wants to be seen as the people builds a container exactly people-sized, then fills it on anniversaries. Supporters call the clearance nation-building; critics mourn the neighbourhoods and the old ceremonial corridor it erased. One breath, both true. The daily flag-raising at sunrise works the same way: soldiers march out of the gate tower, the flag goes up in the dawn wind, and the crowd goes silent.

The politics stays plain. In the middle stands the Monument to the People's Heroes, raised in 1958 to a century of revolutionaries. The square is also where the 1989 student-led protests ended in a military crackdown — an event commemorated abroad and unmentionable in public here, with no plaque and no discussion offered. Expect cameras, bag X-rays and patient police. Photography of the square itself is welcome; photographing the guards up close is not.

Entry is free but reserved: book online ahead, bring your passport, and verify the rules because they shift. Now walk north across the paving, a few hundred metres through the security lanes, to the red wall and the giant portrait ahead.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north across the square toward the red gate tower with the large portrait, about 400 metres. Leave the square through the signposted exit, cross Chang'an Avenue by the underpass (never at street level), and follow the lane to the gate tower entrance.
stops.openingHours: Roughly 05:00 to 22:00 daily with reservation slots; flag-raising at sunrise. Verify times locally.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: TarnishedPath, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Step free at ground level. Climbing the tower means steep stairs; the rostrum balcony is not accessible.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Viewing the tower from outside is free. Climbing to the rostrum is ticketed (about ¥15 at last check); verify at the gate.
stops.insiderTip: Look at the two giant slogan boards flanking the portrait: they have read the same two lines since 1949, and their wording is the whole regime in twelve characters.
stops.name: Tiananmen Gate Tower
stops.narration:
You are looking at the most reproduced facade in China. Tiananmen means the Gate of Heavenly Peace, and the portrait hanging over the central arch is Mao Zedong — the revolutionary leader who founded the People's Republic in 1949 — about six metres tall, repainted by hand every year and replaced when the weather wins.

Here is what this gate is for. In imperial days no commoner passed it; edicts were lowered from its walls in a wooden box for the empire to obey. On October 1, 1949, Mao stood on the balcony above you and proclaimed the new state to the square, and the gate changed jobs: from the emperor's mouth to the republic's rostrum, the place every anniversary parade still salutes. The two white slogan boards say it plainly — long live the People's Republic, long live the unity of the world's peoples — and they have said it since that day. Read them as the building's title page.

Climbing the tower is ticketed, about ¥15 at last check (¥ is the yuan, China's money; the currency is formally called renminbi), but verify at the gate. The climb is steep stairs with no lift. From outside it costs nothing to stand where a billion photographs were taken — mind the traffic wardens, stay on the pavements, and never cross Chang'an Avenue, the great east-west boulevard at its foot, except by the underpass.

From here the palace begins. Head north through the underpass, then follow the walled lane about ten minutes to the U-shaped red fortress ahead. That is the Meridian Gate, and your palace ticket and passport get checked there.
stops.nextStopDirections: Cross Chang'an Avenue by the pedestrian underpass, then walk north along the walled avenue for about 600 metres to the Meridian Gate. Have your Forbidden City booking and passport ready; ticket checks are at this gate.
stops.openingHours: Exterior always viewable. Tower interior roughly 09:00 to 16:30, closed Mondays; verify locally.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: 我乃野云鵤, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Ticket gates are step free, but the gate halls have high wooden thresholds and stone steps throughout. Uneven cobbles underfoot.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Entry is on the Forbidden City ticket (about ¥40 in the November low season, ¥60 in peak months at last check). You must book online days ahead with your passport; there is no walk-up ticket office. Verify everything at booking.
stops.insiderTip: Stand in the central passage and clap once: the U-shaped wings throw the echo back at you like a drum — the architects tuned intimidation.
stops.name: Meridian Gate (Wumen)
stops.narration:
Pass the ticket check and stop inside the gate's shadow. The Meridian Gate — Wumen in Chinese — wraps around you in a U, with two wings reaching out like arms. Three arches pierce it. The middle one was the emperor's alone; princes and officials filed through the sides according to rank. Architecture as org chart.

Now the legend this gate carries, and the correction. Every Chinese speaker knows the phrase ‘dragged out through the Meridian Gate and beheaded’ — it is where period dramas stage executions. It never happened here. Real executions took place at Caishikou, a market crossroads far to the south west. What happened at this gate was theatre of a colder kind: captured rebels were presented, punishments were announced, and the emperor reviewed it all from the tower above. The gate was for displaying power, not blood. Remember that when a guide tells you otherwise.

Logistics, bluntly, because November punishes the unprepared. The palace takes about 80,000 visitors a day and sells out: book online several days ahead with your passport number, expect airport-style bag screening, and dress for wind — the courtyards ahead are stone frying pans in summer and stone freezers now. The ticket is about ¥40 in the low season (¥ is yuan; verify at booking, because prices and rules move), and the whole palace is closed on Mondays except public holidays. Never plan this walk for a Monday.

Walk through the gate and cross the first courtyard to the great three-tiered terrace rising ahead. That is the Hall of Supreme Harmony, the throne's own stage.
stops.nextStopDirections: Pass through the Meridian Gate into the palace, cross the courtyard and the Golden Water bridges, and continue north through the Gate of Supreme Harmony to the great three-tiered marble terrace. The hall on top is the next stop.
stops.openingHours: Same as the Forbidden City: roughly 08:30 to 16:30 in winter, last entry about 15:30. Closed Mondays except holidays; verify at booking.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: N509FZ, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: The terrace is reached only by steep stone staircases; the hall interior is closed and viewed through the doors. High thresholds everywhere.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Covered by the same palace ticket; no separate charge. Verify at booking.
stops.insiderTip: Count the little roof beasts on the hall's ridge: there are ten, the maximum in China, and no other building was allowed that number.
stops.name: Hall of Supreme Harmony
stops.narration:
Climb the terrace steps — slowly, they are steep — and stand at the foot of the biggest throne hall in China. This is the Hall of Supreme Harmony, Taihedian, and it is where the empire showed itself to itself: coronations, imperial weddings, and the New Year audience when the emperor received the bows of thousands of officials ranked across the courtyard below.

Read the roof, because the roof is the rank. It is a double-eaved hip roof — the grandest roof form in the imperial code, reserved for the most important buildings — and along its ridges march ten small glazed beasts, lion and dragon and the rest. Ten is the maximum number in China, and this is the only building that carries all ten. Every other hall in the country makes do with fewer. The message needed no literacy: count the animals, know your place.

Look around the terrace for the bronze furniture and decode it. The sundial and the grain measure say the emperor gives time and food. The crane and tortoise say he wishes the dynasty to live ten thousand years. The bronze vats at the stair corners, once kept full of water, say fire — the palace's terror, since a wooden city this size burned again and again, and this hall alone has been rebuilt several times after lightning and war.

One honest note: you will not go inside. The hall's doors stay shut and the Dragon Throne glints far within, past a forest of red pillars. Peer, photograph through the gap, and accept the distance — subjects never got closer either. Same palace ticket, no extra charge; verify rules at booking.

From here walk due north through the smaller courtyards of the living quarters — quicker than it looks, about ten minutes — to the walled garden at the palace's far end.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north from the terrace through the Gate of Heavenly Purity and the inner-court courtyards, keeping straight for about 700 metres, to the walled garden at the palace's northern end. The garden paths begin just inside its gate.
stops.openingHours: Same as the Forbidden City: roughly 08:30 to 16:30 in winter. Closed Mondays except holidays; verify at booking.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: N509FZ, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Garden paths are mostly level but narrow, with steps up the rockery and at the north gate. Can be slippery with fallen leaves.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Covered by the same palace ticket; no separate charge. Verify at booking.
stops.insiderTip: Find the Hall of Imperial Peace at the garden's centre: its Taoist water-and-fire gods explain why a palace that kept burning prayed at a garden shrine.
stops.name: Imperial Garden
stops.narration:
Step through the gateway and the palace exhales. After a kilometre of symmetry and stone, here are crooked pines, cut-rock hills and paths that deliberately wander. This is the Imperial Garden, Yuhuayuan, the private retreat at the palace's northern tip — barely a tenth of the palace grounds, and the only part built for pleasure rather than ceremony.

Two things here teach the whole palace. First, the piled-rock hill: an artificial mountain of contorted Taihu stones, the kind emperors paid fortunes to drag down the canals from the south. Why pile a mountain inside a garden? Because of feng shui — literally wind-and-water, the old rules for siting buildings so cosmic forces flow kindly. A proper seat faces south to the light with a protective height behind its north. The palace's real northern mountain is the hill waiting across the street; this rockery is its miniature echo, a mountain you can climb in twelve steps.

Second, the Hall of Imperial Peace at the garden's heart, roofed in black glazed tiles. It is a Taoist shrine — Taoism being China's native religion of nature gods, immortals and rituals — dedicated to the gods of water and the north. A wooden palace that burned for centuries put its fire insurance in the garden: pray to water at the safe end of the axis. Emperors drank tea here, wrote poems here, and let the ceremony drop. You can feel why.

The cypresses around you are centuries old, older than the last dynasty. Same palace ticket, no extra charge. When you are done wandering, leave by the north gate — the Gate of Divine Prowess, the palace's back door — cross the street, and climb the hill in front of you.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the garden and exit the palace through the Gate of Divine Prowess (Shenwumen) at its northern end. Cross Jingshan Front Street to the Jingshan Park south entrance (separate small ticket), then follow the stepped path straight up the hill to the summit pavilion.
stops.openingHours: Same as the Forbidden City: roughly 08:30 to 16:30 in winter. Closed Mondays except holidays; verify at booking.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: xiquinhosilva, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: The climb is steep stepped paths with handrails but no step-free route; roughly 100 steps to the summit. Not accessible for wheelchairs.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Jingshan Park charges a small separate entry (about ¥2 at last check). Pay at the south gate; verify locally.
stops.insiderTip: Face south at the pavilion rail and trace the axis with your finger: palace roofs, gate tower, square, Qianmen — the whole morning in one line.
stops.name: Jingshan Summit Pavilion
stops.narration:
Climb — it is steep, take the rails — and come out on the pavilion terrace. Turn south. Below you the palace spreads its golden roofs in perfect rows, and beyond them the gate tower, the square and the Qianmen gate stand on one line to the horizon. You are looking down the Beijing Central Axis, the 7.8-kilometre ceremonial spine the city inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2024. Nowhere else shows it whole. The feng shui rule from the garden makes sense at last: this man-made hill is the protective mountain piled up behind the palace's north, so the throne could face the southern light with solid ground at its back.

The hill keeps one dark story. In 1644, as rebel armies broke through the outer walls, the last Ming emperor — the Ming being the dynasty that built this palace in 1406–20, before the Qing Manchus took it in 1644 — fled here and hanged himself from a locust tree on these slopes. A dynasty that had ruled nearly three centuries ended on a morning walk's worth of ground from its throne. The tree is marked below; people still leave the spot quiet.

This is the end of the axis and the end of the walk. The park ticket was a couple of yuan at the gate — verify locally — and the paths down the east slope are gentler on knees. Go down slowly, find something hot to eat, and remember the shape of the morning: one straight line, from a merchant street to a throne to a hilltop, and a city that still arranges itself around emperors three centuries gone. When you are warm again, the Temple of Heaven waits south — a whole second axis of heaven-worship, for another day.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Descend by the east-slope path for gentler steps, exit through the park's east or south gate, and pick up buses or the subway from there. The Temple of Heaven — heaven-worship on a second axis — is a separate tour for another day.
stops.openingHours: Roughly 06:30 to 20:00 daily; shorter hours in winter. Verify at the gate.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Sakhalinio, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
